> Cohort 3 participants were exposed to short (1 sec) video-clips from the Pain E-motion Faces Database (PEMF) [28].

> Cohort 1 participants were engaged in two tasks.

> Data were split into five parts, with all trials of a given participant assigned to the same fold.

> All participants provided written informed consent prior to the experiment and were compensated for their time.

> Participants completed a two-alternative forced-choice task implemented in MATLAB using the Psychtoolbox library.

> Participants were asked "which face displays the higher degree of pain?"

> Prior to the main task, participants completed a brief training phase to familiarize themselves with the procedure.

> 2) Facial Expressions: Cohort 2 participants were exposed to 24 video-clips selected from the UNBC-McMaster Shoulder Pain Expression Archive Database [6].

> 3) Task: Participants were engaged in a task where they had to quantify the intensity of pain attributed to each of the 24 facial expressions through a VAS ranging from 1 to 10.

> Finally, in the original paradigm, participants were sub-selected based on their sensitivity to selfpain and to their susceptibility to the exertion task.

> As these factors are irrelevant for the present analysis (which focuses exclusively on the assessment of facial expressions), here we included all participants recruited.

> 2) Facial Expressions: Cohort 3 participants were exposed to video-clips from the Pain E-motion Faces Database (PEMF) [7].

> Participants were exposed also to simulated pain expressions (all sub-cohorts) and neutral expressions (sub-cohort 3.1 & 3.4), although these were not taken into consideration in keeping with Cohorts 1-2.

> 2) Facial Expressions: Cohort 1 participants were exposed to the same database of spontaneous expressions of pain, disgust and neutral events.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Assessing others' pain relies heavily on facial expressions, yet how individuals translate observable facial features into pain judgments remains poorly understood.

We combined a retrospective analysis of spontaneous pain expressions across three cohorts (Study 1, N = 398) with a reverse correlation experiment using synthetic facial stimuli (Study 2, N = 63) to investigate which facial muscle contractions (Action Units, AUs) drive pain judgments.

Across the two studies, brow raising (AUs 1-2), brow lowering (AU 4), nose wrinkling/upper lip raising (AUs 9-10), lips corner depressor (AU 15) and mouth aperture were identified as key contributors.
Multivariate pattern analysis from Study 1 indicated that pain judgments rely on a distributed set of facial AUs that partly generalize across independent cohorts and stimulus sets.
Tailored co-engagement analysis from Study 2 identified AU pairs that, when combined, facilitate (AUs 7 + 43) or inhibit (AUs 4 + 9, 10 + 27) pain assessments.

Finally, Study 2 also revealed AU information that were taken into consideration depending on the Sex of the displayed face, although the overall contribution of this factor was modest and no systematic effect was observed in Study 1.
These findings provide a first systematic mapping of the observable facial muscle contractions that drive human pain decoding.
The identified facial features are best interpreted in terms of flexible pain processing, whereby individuals base their inference on distinct, partly-redundant patterns of facial responses.
Assessing others' pain is crucial in many clinical and everyday contexts [1, 2].

text.text: Unlike most medical conditions, pain is difficult to quantify objectively, and is mainly assessed using patients' selfreports and indirect reactions.
Facial responses are particularly informative in this respect, due to both their sensitivity to affect and to their communicative relevance, especially when verbal selfreports are unavailable [3].
text.formatted: Facial responses are particularly informative in this respect, due to both their sensitivity to affect and to their communicative relevance, especially when verbal selfreports are unavailable <ref type="bibr">[3]</ref>.

text.text: Many studies investigated painful expressions through the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) [4], which decomposes facial responses into coordinated muscle groups, or Action Units (AUs).

text.text: Several AUs have been consistently implicated in pain: brow lowering (AU 4), eye narrowing (AU 6/7), nose wrinkling/upper lip raising (AU 9/10), mouth opening (AU 25/26/27) and eyes closing/blinking (AU 43/45) [5, 6].

text.text: Importantly, strong inter-individual variability has also been observed, to the point that some scholars refer to distinct pain expressions, rather than to a single prototypical one [7, 8].

text.text: Most studies investigated pain expressions in terms of encoding (which AUs are engaged during pain?), whereas less is known about decoding (which AU engagements influence observers' assessments?).
Patrick et al. [9] recorded spontaneous reactions to electric stimulation, and found that movements associated with AUs 4 and 45 predicted observers' intensity ratings.

text.text: Other studies applied visual noise (reverse correlation [10, 11]) or spatial filtering [11, 12] to the face images, identifying which visual features explained pain judgments in a fully data-driven fashion.

text.text: This approach, however, characterizes facial information only in terms of regions (eyes, mouth), rather than underlying musculature.
To our knowledge, no study has combined the methodological strengths of reverse correlation [10, 11] with a careful assessment of the role played by facial muscle contractions.

text.text: Meta-analyses and multi-center studies document sex and gender disparities in how pain is acknowledged and treated, with females being more likely to have their symptoms underestimated and less likely to receive medications [13] [14] [15] [16].

text.text: The literature on facial expression has also addressed this issue: albeit adult females generally exhibit stronger facial muscular responses to painful stimuli than males [17], findings on the decoding are mixed, with some suggesting that female facial expressions are associated with lower ratings than male expressions (even when controlling carefully for the intensity of facial contraction) [18, 19], and others showing instead opposite effects or no sex differences [20] [21] [22].

However, this possibility remains untested.
Here, we investigated which facial AUs observers rely on to evaluate pain.
First, we ran a largescale analysis on multiple datasets to examine observers' evaluations of spontaneous facial reactions to pain.

Second, we devised a modified reverse correlation task [10, 11] using synthetic expressions with pseudo-random AU engagement, enabling direct inference about the contribution of facial musculature to observers' judgments.

Cohort 1 participants were engaged in two tasks.

The first was a classification task, where they had to assess whether each facial expression displayed "pain" or another state ("disgust" or "neutral"), by pressing a key associated with the chosen label.
The second was a rating task, where they were asked to quantify the degree of unpleasantness experienced by the person in the video.

Ratings were provided using a visual analogue scale (VAS) where the two endpoints were labeled as "neutral" and "extremely unpleasant", and a cursor could be moved along the scale by pressing two different keys.
Participants from Cohorts 2 & 3 were engaged in a task where they had to quantify the intensity of pain attributed to each facial expression through a VAS ranging from "no pain" to "extreme pain".

text.text: Specifically, multivariate models allow estimating the involvement of AUs, not only in terms of engagement vs. non-engagement (classification models) but also in terms of strength of contraction (regression models).
For each frame of each video-clip, we obtained regression estimates for relevant AUs.
The only exception was the estimation of eye blinks (AU 45).
As these movements are usually interpreted as an all-or-none response, a classification-based estimate of this AU was chosen instead.

Although the original databases were subjected to human FACS scoring, this approach differed in terms of the measure assessed (only occurrence vs. also intensity) and in terms of resolution (cumulative engagement across the clip vs. frame-by-frame analysis) making it difficult to compare results from the three cohorts.
In this respect, OpenFace estimates have the advantage of providing the same AU assessment for all video-clips.
Supplementary Information reports the results of a follow-up validation analysis, where the human scoring was compared with OpenFace estimates.
For all databases, there was good overall agreement between human FACS coding and OpenFace output for homologous AUs.
However, in line with prior studies comparing human and computerbased AU scoring [26], we also found cross-predictions between dissimilar AUs (see Supplementary Figure 1 for more details).

text.text: Having established that OpenFace output shows fairly good agreement with human FACS scoring, we took the Area Under the Curve of the OpenFace output as a measure of the cumulative effect of each AU within the whole clip.

In particular, we followed studies showing the benefit of combining AUs underlying similar facial movements together, both when assessing the reliability of algorithms for facial feature extraction [31], and in the human coding of the facial expression of pain [5, 7, 8].

For the purpose of this work, we chose as dependent variables individual judgments about pain or unpleasantness.
Specifically, for Cohort 1 we took unpleasantness ratings (on a VAS) and pain classifications (provided as a dichotomic response), whereas for Cohorts 2-3 we took pain ratings (on a VAS).

text.text: As independent variables, we chose the 13 AU estimates provided by the OpenFace algorithm.
Additionally, we controlled for the Sex of the participants (between-subjects factor: Sex) and that of the person displayed in the videos (withinsubjects factor: FaceSex).
We ran linear mixed models (LMMs) where single-trial judgments were assessed as a function of AU engagement, Sex, FaceSex and their interaction.
The identity of the participants and that of the video-displayed person were specified as random factors (see Supplementary Information for full details on the random structure).
Significance of the fixed effects was calculated with a Type II Analysis of Variance using the Satterthwaite approximation of degrees of freedom [33].

text.text: We also adopted a multivariate approach, and trained Random Forest (RF) regression (for unpleasantness/pain ratings; Cohorts 1-3) and classification (for pain classifications; Cohort 1) to predict participants' assessments of facial expressions.
Random Forest involves the implementation of decision trees, which perform recursive partitioning of the facial (feature) space to lead to a non-linear predictive model.

Because decision trees are susceptible to small perturbations in the dataset, RF reduces prediction variance by aggregating the outcomes from trees fitted to bootstrap resamples of the original dataset [34].
text.formatted: Because decision trees are susceptible to small perturbations in the dataset, RF reduces prediction variance by aggregating the outcomes from trees fitted to bootstrap resamples of the original dataset <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref>.

text.text: To ensure out-of-sample prediction, a five-fold cross-validation scheme was implemented on a per-subject basis.
Data were split into five parts, with all trials of a given participant assigned to the same fold.
Data from one fold were then predicted using a model trained on the remaining four folds.
The analysis was run as implemented in the randomForest package in R using 1000 trees per model.
Model performance for classification outcomes was summarized using classification accuracy (proportion of correct responses) and d-prime (d') [35].
text.formatted: Model performance for classification outcomes was summarized using classification accuracy (proportion of correct responses) and d-prime (d') <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref>.

text.text: For continuous outcomes, two primary evaluation measures were used: the fixed-effect slope (b) obtained from an LMM, assessing the agreement between observed and predicted scores; and the mean squared error (MSE), averaged first within and then across participants.
To assess whether model performance exceeded chance levels, permutation tests were performed using 1000 data shuffles of the original datasets.

Critical thresholds were defined as the 95 𝑡ℎ percentile of the null distribution for classification accuracy, d' and regression slopes (in order to ensure greater-than-chance prediction), and the 5 𝑡ℎ percentile for MSE (in order to ensure lower-than-chance error).
After evaluating model performance using cross-validation, the final model was refitted using the entire dataset to extract variable importance scores.
Importance measures included the average decrease in accuracy for classification models, and the percentage MSE increase.

The importance estimate for each feature was also validated using permutation techniques, in order to identify features whose contribution to the overall prediction was greater than the one observed under null hypothesis.
Finally, regression models were run and also validated across cohorts, in order to establish whether a model tailored to one cohort could also predict responses in a different cohort.
For each pair of cohorts, models were trained and validated across two independent folds, in each of which the model was trained on one cohort and tested in the other one.

This retrospective analysis of three independent cohorts allowed us to identify a core set of AUs that significantly influence participants' pain-related judgments.

In the univariate analysis we found no core set of facial responses implicated in all cohorts, although AUs 1-2, 9-10, 15, and 25-26 were observed in all analyses except that of Cohort 3 which, instead, implicated only AU 4 (Figure 1).

text.text: It should be stressed that univariate results were constrained by correction for multiple compar-isons, which considers as relevant only the most pronounced influences, disregarding weaker (but potentially converging across cohorts) effects.

Multivariate pattern analysis, instead, identified a higher degree of cross-cohort convergence (Table 2) suggesting that individuals assess pain using a partially shared set of AU patterns that univariate analyses failed to capture.

text.text: Importantly, however, cross-cohort predictive performance, albeit higher than chance, is substantially lower than the one obtained when modeling each cohort alone.

It is possible that AU contributions in this analysis are context-sensitive and influenced by idiosyncratic cohort characteristics, task structure, or differences in the facial expression databases (luminance, duration, angle, etc).
Furthermore, previous work on pain expression encoding stresses how AU engagement tends to co-occur based on distinct patterns of pain reactions [7, 8].
text.formatted: Furthermore, previous work on pain expression encoding stresses how AU engagement tends to co-occur based on distinct patterns of pain reactions <ref type="bibr">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr">8]</ref>.

text.text: Hence, although all datasets are characterized by facial reactions to pain, these do not necessarily depict exactly the same muscular information.
It is therefore not surprising that, in some cases, AUs 9/10 appear more relevant (Cohorts 1-2), whereas in others it is AU 4 that best explains behavior (Cohort 3).

It is important to stress that, as multiple pain-relevant AUs might co-engage following the same painful event [5] [6] [7] [8], it is often difficult to distinguish those AUs that are most relevant for pain decoding from those that are merely part of the same overall expression but are not actually taken into consideration by the observer.

text.text: Overall, albeit relevant from an ecological point of view, these results underscore the inherent limitations associated with investigating pain expression decoding through spontaneous pain reactions, and call for alternative approaches where AU information is administered in a randomized (or pseudo-randomized) fashion.

text.text: This cohort was composed of N = 63 individuals (40 females, 22 males, 1 sex non-reported; mean age = 25.65 ± 4.17 years).
All participants provided written informed consent prior to the experiment and were compensated for their time.

The study was conducted at the Center for Mind/Brain Sciences (CIMeC) of the University of Trento, in accordance with the local regulations and the "Comitato Etico per la Ricerca" of the University of Trento.
The facial expression stimuli used in this study were generated using FACSGen software [36] to create synthetic expressions with predefined AU engagements.

text.text: In particular, in FACSGen each AU is implemented with its own independent "blend shape", which was in turn sculpted by graphic designers (the company "Trait d'Esprit", http://www.traitdesprit.ch/) on the basis of reference pictures and videos, and interactive validation with certified FACS coders [36].

text.text: Here, we created an initial picture database of 400 facial expressions, from 20 distinct identities (10 males and 10 females) each associated with 20 unique facial configurations.
Each picture was created with a unique pseudorandomized set of AU engagements, where each blend shape can be assigned an index ranging from 0 (not engaged at all) to 1 (full facial response).
It is important to underscore that AU blend shapes were created on an individual basis, and subsequently mixed together using linear interpolation to obtain a full facial expression.

It is possible that combining different (independently validated) blend shapes might lead to implausible expressions, especially for AUs with opposing effects (e.g., lip pucker AU 18 and lip opener AU 20) which seldom occur in the same expression.
To minimize this possibility, AU configurations were generated using constrained pseudo randomization.
First, we focused on a set of 23 AUs (i.e., 1-2, 4-7, 9-12, 14-18, 20, 22-27 & 43) based on those available in the FACSGen software.
text.formatted: First, we focused on a set of 23 AUs (i.e., 1-2, 4-7, 9-12, 14-18, 20, 22-27 & 43) based on those available in the FACSGen software.

text.text: For each picture, we randomly chose two AUs to be fully engaged (1), two partially engaged (0.6) and one minimally engaged (0.1), whereas all the others were set to 0.
This procedure ensured that all stimuli were matched in terms of total activation (as assigned by the software) while varying its allocation across facial movements.
We then discarded the configurations with co-engagement of AUs with opposing effects (e.g., AUs 1-2 & 4, AUs 12 & 15, AUs 18 & 20).
text.formatted: We then discarded the configurations with co-engagement of AUs with opposing effects (e.g., AUs 1-2 & 4, AUs 12 & 15, AUs <ref type="bibr">18 & 20)</ref>.

text.text: The only exception was the co-engagement of AUs 1 & 4, as FACSGen has an ad hoc blend shape which combines the two movements in a plausible fashion.
text.formatted: The only exception was the co-engagement of AUs 1 & 4, as FACSGen has an ad hoc blend shape which combines the two movements in a plausible fashion.

text.text: In this specific case, if these AUs were co-engaged under the same parameters (e.g., both at 0.6), the random configuration was not discarded.
All discarded images were replaced with a new randomization until the desired 400 stimuli were obtained.
All resulting images were then visually inspected to ensure they represented plausible facial expressions.
Participants completed a two-alternative forced-choice task implemented in MATLAB using the Psychtoolbox library.
On each trial, two randomly selected facial expressions from the same identity were simultaneously presented side by side on a computer screen.
Participants were asked "which face displays the higher degree of pain?"
and were instructed to answer by pressing either the left or right arrow key on the keyboard (Figure 2B).
text.formatted: and were instructed to answer by pressing either the left or right arrow key on the keyboard (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">2B</ref>).

text.text: Prior to the main task, participants completed a brief training phase to familiarize themselves with the procedure.
The main experimental phase consisted of 200 trials in total, corresponding to 10 trials for each of the 20 different identities.
Reaction times and selected responses were recorded for each trial.
The overall experimental session lasted approximately 15 minutes.
While Study 1 included realistic expressions with naturally co-engaged AUs, here each specific facial movement was pseudo-randomly parameterized.
Hence, we did not combine those AUs underlying common macro-movements.
Instead, each of the 23 AUs was analyzed as independent predictor.
Each trial is characterized by the presence of two randomly-selected pictures from the same identity, each associated with a unique facial configuration of AU engagements.
In all analyses, AU parameters (originally recorded as a proportion ranging from 0 to 1) were logittransformed following the same procedure as in Study 1.

In this framework, to establish whether any of the 23 AUs were predictive of participants' judgments, we considered right/left choices as a dichotomous dependent variable: specifically, trials where the right picture was deemed more painful were labeled as "1", whereas trials the left picture was deemed more painful were labeled as "0".
As main predictor of interest, we considered the differential AU parameters obtained by subtracting the values associated with the left stimulus from those associated with the right stimulus.
This resulted in a differential facial configuration, with positive values reflecting those AUs more engaged in the right face, and negative values reflecting those AUs more engaged in the left face.

We ran Generalized LMMs with a binomial distribution and Laplace approximation, with choice as dependent variable, differential AU, Sex and FaceSex as fixed factors, and the identity of participants and of the displayed person as random factors (see Supplementary Information for full random structure).
Significance of fixed effects was established through Type II Analysis of Deviance and Wald 𝜒 2 statistics as for Study 1.
This model was repeated for all 23 AUs, and effects were considered significant if associated with an 𝛼 < .05 Bonferroni corrected for multiple comparisons.
text.formatted: This model was repeated for all 23 AUs, and effects were considered significant if associated with an 𝛼 < .05 Bonferroni corrected for multiple comparisons.

text.text: We also assessed potential co-engagement effects, that is, AU combinations that were more likely to trigger pain classification when engaged together.
This analysis was carried out through the same Generalized LMM approach described above, except that we did not model only information about one AU.

Instead, we modeled simultaneously the differential parameters of two separate AUs, their interaction term (described as the right -left difference of their products) as well as further high-level modulations of Sex/FaceSex (see Supplementary Information for full details).
The interaction between the two AUs was the main predictor of interest in the co-engagement analysis.
If two AUs contribute to pain judgments in a totally additive fashion, then the interaction term should be = 0.
Positive interactions suggest that AUs co-presence further increases the likelihood of pain classifications beyond the contribution of each AU alone.
Negative interactions suggest instead a sub-additive integration.

The analysis was carried out for every possible AU combination (253 potential pairings), although due to the pseudo-randomization procedure implemented for stimuli generation, some AUs never co-occurred (see above) and only 246 pairings were conducted.
Results were considered significant if they survived Bonferroni correction for all repeated tests.

text.text: This study provides novel, convergent evidence that pain judgments rely on a distributed set of observable facial muscle contractions (Action Units, AUs).

Combining a retrospective analysis of spontaneous pain expressions across three different cohorts (Study 1) with a reverse correlation experiment using synthetic facial stimuli (Study 2), we confirmed the key contribution of inner brow raising (AU 1), brow lowering (AU 4), nose wrinkling (AU 9), upper lip raising (AU 10), lip corner depressor (AU 15) and mouth opening (AUs 25-26 in Study 1; AU 27 in Study 2) to pain assessment.
Multivariate pattern analysis indicated that pain judgments rely on a distributed set of facial AUs, partially consistent across cohorts (Study 1).

Co-engagement analysis (Study 2) suggests that pain classifications are also explainable in terms of AU combinations (e.g., AU 7-43), rather than isolated facial responses, alongside evidence that some AUs interfere with each other's contributions (e.g., AUs 4-9, 10-27).

To our knowledge this is the first investigation of the mental representation of pain expressions through the lens of the Facial Action Coding System [4], showing that individuals draw on pain-relevant information flexibly, exploiting distinct, partly-redundant patterns of facial responses.

text.text: Our findings are not necessarily incompatible with this interpretation, although the presence of female-preferential AU patterns speaks more in favor of variability and flexibility in the decoding strategy, with partially different facial information considered relevant for male and female expressions.

It could be tempting to relate our findings to prior evidence of sex disparities in clinical settings [13] [14] [15] [16], as caregivers might interpret female pain through an ad hoc facial template that makes them more prone to underestimating symptoms.

text.text: Albeit this is an intriguing possibility, clinical pain assessment is not based exclusively on facial decoding, but on a comprehensive evaluation of behavioral reactions, verbal reports and contextual information.

text.text: It is important also to underscore that Study 1 describes AU modulations that were conditional to the sex of the observed face.
These, however, were inconsistent between the different cohorts as well as with those observed in Study 2.

The variability in Study 1 effects most likely reflects idiosyncratic properties of the three databases, such as orientation and luminosity, as well as the inter-individual differences in pain sensitivity and responsiveness.

In this perspective, the synthetic stimuli from Study 2 provide more reliable AU effects, as the software used was optimized to provide clearly recognizable AU engagements regardless of the face to which they are applied [36].

text.text: Still, it is important to underscore that multivariate Random Forest classification in Study 2 confirms that the inclusion of FaceSex had trivial impact on the overall prediction of participants' choices.

Emotion research has repeatedly debated whether affective inference from facial reactions relies on prototypical template-matching or, alternatively, on decomposing the expression into idiosyncratic and variable combinations of emotion constituents, such as contextual appraisals [38].

text.text: Caution is warranted in extending this debate to pain, which previous studies have rarely addressed directly.

This being said, our findings point to flexibility and variability in facial decoding strategies, with multiple AUs interfering with one another in the degree to which they convey pain information, and to an extent also sex-preferential facial patterns.
Hence, pain decoding appears to rely on multiple, redundant face patterns, something that is more in line with a multicomponential organization of the pain response.
Interestingly, multi-componential accounts could offer an explanation as to why participants focus on some facial cues over others.

Indeed, prior work links AU 1 engagement and mouth opening to appraisals of novelty, and AUs 4, 9 and 15 engagement to appraisals of unpleasantness and low control [39] [40] [41], suggesting that participants may have read facial signs that are informative of something "bad" or "sudden".

text.text: As these assessments are not specific to pain, future studies should test whether these findings generalize to other affective experiences.
Despite its advantages, the reverse correlation task implemented here has some limitations.
First, the FACSGen software [36] used to generate the stimuli was optimized for isolated AU engagements and emotional expressions, rather than random AU parameter assignments.

text.text: To minimize potential artifacts, we used constrained pseudo-randomization to avoid selected combinations of facial movements with opposing effects and visually checked that each stimulus represented a plausible facial expression (see Methods).
However, some AU combinations may appear different on synthetic avatars than on real faces.

Second, to minimize the risk that participants' choices were driven by overall engagement (rather than specific facial configurations), all stimuli in Study 2 were created with matched total AU activation parameters, while varying its allocation across facial movements.
However, controlling overall activation during stimulus generation does not necessarily ensure that perceived expressiveness or the magnitude of visible movement is matched.
Furthermore, allocating activation to one AU necessarily restricted its allocation to others, introducing dependencies among AUs.
Consequently, the contribution of each AU to pain classifications should not be interpreted in absolute terms, but rather in relation to all other available facial information.
Notwithstanding these limitations, our study provides a first clear mapping of the facial muscle contractions that drive individual pain judgments.
These findings provide strong support for the idea that pain decoding is represented flexibly, relying on variable, partly-redundant patterns of facial responses.

text.text: In summary, 68 individuals (aged 18-61) were recorded under standardized laboratory conditions while displaying four types of facial expressions: neutral, simulated pain, and two types of spontaneous pain expressions elicited through distinct nociceptive procedures: tonic pressure stimulation via an algometer and phasic heat stimulation via a CO 2 laser.

From these recordings, short dynamic video-clips of 1 sec were extracted to capture the peak of the painful expression, resulting in a database of 272 validated micro-clips, which have been normatively rated for pain intensity, valence, and arousal by over 500 participants from multiple European universities.

For the purpose of this analysis, we focused on data from a subsample of 28 video-clips displaying spontaneous pain expressions as induced by either an algometer (11 clips) or CO 2 laser-stimulations (17 clips).
All these clips were edited to be 1 sec long and sound free.

Participants were exposed also to simulated pain expressions (all sub-cohorts) and neutral expressions (sub-cohort 3.1 & 3.4), although these were not taken into consideration in keeping with Cohorts 1-2.

text.text: 3) Task: Participants viewed each video clip and subsequently assessed the facial expression according to two dimensions: pain intensity and authenticity.
The first question was: "Rate how much pain you perceive in the expression on a scale from 1 (no pain) to 10 (extreme pain)".
The second question was: "Rate how authentic the expression seems on a scale from 1 (not authentic at all) to 10 (completely authentic)".
In sub-cohort 3.2, 3.3 and 3.4, the videos were presented following a predictive cue of variable intensity and uncertainty.
However, the role of this predictive information was not taken into account in the present study.
As for the other cohorts, the potential confounding effects in the experimental design were controlled during the analysis.
To establish that OpenFace estimates of AU engagement were indeed comparable to that from certified human FACS scorers, we ran a validation analysis for each database.
For cohort 1, two certified FACS scorers evaluated a subgroup of short clips (6 painful, 6 disgusting and 6 neutral) by selecting AU onset/offset time and the intensity (on a scale from 1 to 5).

text.text: Differently from cohorts 1-2 where scoring occurred on a frame-by-frame basis and included both information about engagement and estimated intensity, here coders only assessed AU occurrence.
Furthermore, this procedure was conducted at the whole-clip level, meaning coders judged the overall presence of AUs across the entire video, rather than in each isolated frame.
Within this framework, an AU was considered as engaged if at least four out of the six coders agreed on its occurrence [7].
text.formatted: Within this framework, an AU was considered as engaged if at least four out of the six coders agreed on its occurrence <ref type="bibr">[7]</ref>.

text.text: We then compared the human scores with OpenFace output from the same clip subselection.
In cohorts 1-2 clips, for each AU, and for each video, we assessed the consistency between the time-course of the human scoring and OpenFace output.

Furthermore, we followed studies showing the benefit of combining AUs underlying similar facial movements together, both when assessing the reliability of algorithms for facial feature extraction [8], and in the human coding of the facial expression of pain [9]- [11].
text.formatted: Furthermore, we followed studies showing the benefit of combining AUs underlying similar facial movements together, both when assessing the reliability of algorithms for facial feature extraction <ref type="bibr">[8]</ref>, and in the human coding of the facial expression of pain <ref type="bibr">[9]</ref>- <ref type="bibr">[11]</ref>.

text.text: Hence, we decided to treat as equivalent facial AUs related to the eyebrows raising (AUs 1 & 2), eye narrowing (AUs 6 & 7), nose wrinkling (AUs 9 & 10), lips tightening/pressing (AUs 23 & 24), mouth opening (AUs 25, 26 & 27) and eye closing/blinks (AUs 43 & 45).
text.formatted: Hence, we decided to treat as equivalent facial AUs related to the eyebrows raising (AUs 1 & 2), eye narrowing (AUs 6 & 7), nose wrinkling (AUs 9 & 10), lips tightening/pressing (AUs 23 & 24), mouth opening (AUs <ref type="bibr">25, 26 & 27)</ref> and eye closing/blinks (AUs 43 & 45).

text.text: Please note that, whereas human coding provides estimates of any potential AUs, OpenFace output is constrained to an AU subselection, and specifically has no estimates of AUs 24, 27 and 43.
Thus, while human coding of mouth opening was based on AUs 25, 26 and 27, OpenFace homologue is based only on AUs 25 & 26 (AU 27 movements are likely classified by the algorithm as either 25 or 26).
text.formatted: Thus, while human coding of mouth opening was based on AUs 25, 26 and 27, OpenFace homologue is based only on AUs 25 & 26 (AU 27 movements are likely classified by the algorithm as either 25 or 26).

text.text: In a similar vein, whereas human coding of lips tightening is obtained from AUs 23/24, OpenFace homologue is derived on AU23.

Finally, whereas human coding of eye closure/blinks is obtained by combining both AUs 43/45, OpenFace homologue is based only on AU 45 (the algorithm most likely does not distinguish between eye closures and blinks).

In Cohort 3, where human FACS scoring was not carried out at a frame-by-frame level, we took comprehensive measure of each algorithm-based AU across the whole clip (the Area under the curve and, for AU 45, the percentage engagement within the whole clip) and modelled as a function of human-scored engagement from the original study.

We then ran a Linear Mixed Model (LMM) with the OpenFace estimates as dependent variable, the intensity of the homologous AUs information from FACS scorers as continuous predictor, and the identity of the participant in the video as random factor (with random intercept and slope for the human score).
A simpler random structure (characterised only by random intercept) was chosen in case of nonconvergence.

Given that in cohorts 1-2, the prediction of OpenFace estimates of AU 45 was expressed as a dichotomic variable (reflecting engagement vs. non-engagement), we exploited instead a Generalized LMM with a binomial distribution and Laplace approximation.
The LMMs were run following the same processing pipeline described in the main text.
Supplementary Figure 1 reports the results of the analysis in matrix form, with each cell reflecting the prediction of one OpenFace AU from a human scored one.

text.text: Effects highlighted are considered statistically significant.

Predictions from homologous AUs (e.g., Open Face AU 4 estimate predicted by human scored AU 4 engagement) were considered significant if associated with α ≤ 0.05 one-tailed with the hypothesis constrained for positive relationships.
All other predictions were considered significant if associated with α ≤ 0.05 two-tailed with no directional hypothesis.
Overall, this validation analysis shows good agreement between human FACS coding and OpenFace output for homologous AUs.
The only notable exceptions were AUs 1/2, 6/7 and 23 (Cohort 1) and AU 20 (Cohort 3) for which OpenFace estimates could not be predicted by homologous human scores.
Additionally, many cross-predictions between dissimilar AUs are observed, with both negative and positive directions (see Dirupo et al., [4] for in-depth commentary on this issue).

text.text: These recordings were subsequently used to create short video-clips of variable duration (average 7.61 sec) where the same individuals displayed either a painful, disgusting or neutral expression, and the two negative experiences were matched for unpleasantness from the point of view of both the video-recorded person (from self-rating) and an independent sample of observers.

3) Task: Participants were engaged in two tasks.
The first was a classification task, where they had to assess whether each facial expression displayed "pain", "disgust" or a "neutral" state, by pressing a key associated with the chosen label.
The second was a rating task, where they were asked to quantify the degree of unpleasantness experienced by the person in the video.

The evaluation happened through a visual analogue scale (VAS) where the two extremities were labeled as "neutral" and "extremely unpleasant", and a cursor could be moved along the scale by pressing two different keys.
In sub-cohorts 1.1 & 1.5 the two tasks were implemented sequentially, namely participants first saw the facial expressions, then classified it and subsequently rated the associated unpleasantness.
